title: A Wild Thanksgiving: Storms, Blackouts and a Delayed Parade
summary:
Thanksgiving week brought wild weather to much of the United States. A huge storm stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan, leaving almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening. At the worst point, more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and other states had no electricity, though power was partly back on by early Friday.

Travel took a hit, too. More than 400 flights were cancelled on Thursday, and more than 2,000 were delayed, during one of the busiest travel times of the year. About 81.5 million people were expected to travel between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA. Driving was hard as well, with heavy rain in some places and snow and ice in others.

Flooding hit several areas. Parts of Old Town Alexandria in Virginia and Atlantic City in New Jersey were flooded, with close to 2 to 3 feet of water in some low-lying areas of Atlantic City. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington, D.C., area on Friday, in effect until 6 p.m. Eastern time, and warned people not to drive through water of unknown depth.

Out west, strong waves and high tides known as King Tides battered the California coast, and part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday. In New York City, Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record, with 1.82 inches of rain.

The weather even moved the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. For the first time in its history, the parade was postponed, to Saturday, because strong winds made it unsafe to fly the giant balloons. Around 11,000 people take part, mostly volunteers. Saturday's parade is the 100th, with 100 balloons, including eight new ones such as Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer's Apprentice.

Meanwhile, shoppers headed into Black Friday. The National Retail Federation expects about 183 million shoppers and more than $1 trillion in November and December holiday sales. The top three children's toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.
why_it_matters: Big storms can change holiday plans for millions of people at once, cutting power, cancelling travel and flooding streets — and knowing how to stay safe, like never driving through floodwater, matters for everyone.

background_read: Thanksgiving is a big American holiday in late November, when many families travel to spend the day together, so it is one of the busiest travel weeks of the year.
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City is a famous yearly event with giant balloons, floats and marching bands, and it is usually held on Thanksgiving morning.
Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, when many shops offer big sales and crowds of people go out to start their holiday shopping.
King Tides are extra-high tides that happen a few times a year when the sun, moon and Earth line up, and they can push seawater over beaches and low coastal roads.
